subChunks.title: Why Log & Log Levels

storyBeats.text: Eldrin reviews the incident report from last night's spell failure. The log is a jumble of println statements with no timestamps, no severity markers, no class names.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A log without structure is noise. A structured log is a story: when this happened, where in the codebase, how severe it was. That is the difference between a System.out.println and a proper logging statement.

storyBeats.label: Structured logging

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: In production you use SLF4J with a Logback implementation. In that world: TRACE for the minutest detail, DEBUG for developer diagnostics, INFO for normal operation milestones, WARN for unexpected-but-recoverable events, ERROR for failures that need attention.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a Logger named "SpellLogger". Log one INFO message "Spell cast: Fireball" and one WARNING "Low mana!". Configure it to log to console using a ConsoleHandler set to Level.ALL.
guidedPractice.hint: Set logger.setUseParentHandlers(false) to avoid duplicate output, then add a ConsoleHandler.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Why is System.out.println inadequate for production logging? Describe the five main log levels and when you would use each.

questions.prompt: Which log level indicates a condition that might cause problems but from which the application recovered?
questions.explanation: WARN indicates unexpected situations that the application handled but that deserve attention. ERROR/SEVERE means a failure requiring immediate action.

subChunks.title: SLF4J, Logback & Best Practices

storyBeats.text: Eldrin reveals the Academy's professional logging grimoire — SLF4J, the façade that speaks to any logging library underneath.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: SLF4J is a layer of abstraction. Your code only knows SLF4J. Logback, Log4j, JUL — the actual implementation — can be swapped without changing a single line of your application code. This is the bridge pattern in practice.

storyBeats.label: SLF4J pattern

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The curly-brace placeholders are critical. String concatenation in a debug statement runs even when the debug level is disabled. With {} placeholders, the message is only formatted if the level is active — sometimes a significant performance win.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Demonstrate the logging pattern using java.util.logging. Log at INFO and WARNING level, and demonstrate that a FINE-level message doesn't appear when the level is set to INFO.
guidedPractice.hint: Set handler level to Level.INFO. A log.fine() call should be filtered out.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is the advantage of using {} placeholders in SLF4J logging over string concatenation?

questions.prompt: Why should you use log.debug("Value: {}", computeHeavy()) instead of log.debug("Value: " + computeHeavy())?
options: computeHeavy() is only called if DEBUG level is active
The first version logs faster always
String concatenation doesn't work with loggers
The second version always throws an exception
questions.answer: computeHeavy() is only called if DEBUG level is active
questions.explanation: With string concatenation, computeHeavy() always executes even if DEBUG logging is disabled. With {} placeholders, the argument is only evaluated when the message is actually going to be logged.

questions.prompt: SLF4J is a logging implementation — it writes log statements to files and the console.
questions.explanation: SLF4J is a facade (API only). The actual writing is done by a backing implementation (Logback, Log4j2, JUL). You program against SLF4J so you can swap implementations without changing your code.
